text: 16h Business has a short term thinking problem. But it rarely looks like one. It often looks like a win: a quick fix, another integration, a solution that works just fine for now. It’s how we’ve built Adyen: a single platform designed to grow with our customers instead of being stitched together. Payments shouldn’t just be something that works. author: thejustinwelsh
text:
Nobody gets to approve how I spend my days.

That's the rule I built my whole business around.

I never want to ask another adult for permission to:

Take a vacation.
Go to a ballgame.
Spend time with my wife.
Read in the middle of the day.
Take a day off for any reason.

This very specific freedom has shaped nearly every business decision I've made for the last 7 years.

I could have built some big team of growth gurus, newsletter marketers, operations people, customer support, and a few layers of management.

Or chased more revenue, a monster valuation, more media coverage, and a more "impressive" company.

Instead, I kept the business small enough to manage with my wife.

No employees.
No office politics.
No unnecessary complexity.
No calendar filled with someone else's priorities.

That decision came with tradeoffs, of course.

The business probably could have grown a lot faster.

I would have likely sold more products, appeared on more podcasts and shows, or received more national recognition.

And those things can be incredibly valuable.

But they're not valuable enough for me to exchange control of my time for them.

If you're building something of your own, decide what freedom you actually want before you decide how big your business should become.

Otherwise, it's remarkably easy to create a successful business that gives you a lot less of the life you wanted.

This approach helped me build my little one-person business to $15M in profit and do it my way.

author: airbnb
text:
Istanbul is famous for its outsized cat population who you’ll find roaming free, keeping watch, and mingling with the humans. Meet the cats who rule the city.

By breakfast, the cats are already making the rounds. In Istanbul, they turn up in cafés, markets, bookstores, waterfronts and anywhere people gather.

Istanbul’s official visitor guide gives cats top billing and calls them the “Royalty of Istanbul.”

Istanbul’s cats are independent by design. Most don’t belong to one person, and they’re perfectly happy picking their own lookout points, routes and favorite corners.

Istanbul is often cited as home to one of the largest concentrated street-cat populations in the world.

If there’s a spot to claim, a cat has probably claimed it first. What’s ours is theirs.

Istanbul’s cats are professional photobombers. They show up in wedding photos, tourist’s shots, and plenty of camera rolls they weren’t invited into.

Istanbul helps take care of its street cats with veterinary care, vaccinations and dedicated “paw parks” where animals have space to play. Resist the urge to scoop one up and take it with you. Some have entire neighborhoods looking after them.

An entire film was made about the cats of Istanbul. According to the director, “The real soul of the city is actually, I think, the cats.”
